about.title: The One-Page Medical Sheet for the ER
about.length_note: About 12 minutes. This class has six short parts and a fill-in template. You can stop after any beat and pick up again. Filling in your own sheet will take longer than the class itself, so treat that as homework.

sources.title: Taking someone with dementia to the emergency department? Expert advice to help ease the stress
Emergency Information Forms and Emergency Preparedness for Children With Special Health Care Needs

say.text: Today we make one page. It tells ER staff the things a person cannot say for themselves.

show.text: One page that speaks up for the person

say.text: Know this first. The page does not replace the person's own doctors, and it does not replace a hands-on first-aid or CPR class.

show.text: A helper, not a replacement

say.text: Why a page at all? ER staff usually do not know the person. If the person cannot speak, nobody can fill the gaps.

show.text:
ER staff do not know the history
The person may not be able to tell them
The page tells them first

say.text: Pediatric and emergency doctors' groups warn that missing information can mean delays, extra tests and serious errors. They made a form for children with special health needs. The same idea works for adults.

show.text: Delays, unnecessary tests, and sometimes serious errors

ask.q: Why does a one-page sheet help in an ER?
ask.right: The staff do not know the person, and the person may not be able to tell them.
wrong: It replaces the person's own doctors.
It means you do not need to call 911.
It is only needed for children.
ask.why: The sheet carries the person's story to staff who have never met them. It does not replace doctors or 911.

say.text: Keep it to one page, in big plain print. Short is easier to read in a hurry. We will build six parts.

show.text:
1. Who and how to reach
2. How the person communicates
3. Allergies
4. Medicines and doses
5. Conditions and doctors
6. What is normal, and who decides

say.text: Start at the top with the name, the name the person likes to be called, the date of birth, and the date you last updated the page.

show.text:
Name: Sam (made-up example)
Likes to be called: Sam
Date of birth: ____
Page updated: ____

say.text: Part one: how does the person say yes and no? People do it in many ways. Write down exactly what this person does.

show.text:
YES could be: a nod, thumbs up, a blink, looking up, a tap.
NO could be: a head shake, thumbs down, closing the eyes, looking down.

say.text: For Sam, you might write: Yes is one blink. No is two blinks. Use the signals the person really uses, not the ones from this list.

show.text:
Sam says YES: one blink
Sam says NO: two blinks (example only)

ask.q: What belongs on the sheet about yes and no?
ask.right: The exact signals this person uses.
wrong: The signals most people use, from a list.
Nothing. Staff will work it out.
ask.why: Each person's signals are their own. If staff know them, they can ask questions and get real answers.

say.text: Next: signs of pain or distress. If a person cannot say 'it hurts', what do you see and hear? Write that down.

show.text:
Face: ____
Sounds: ____
Body: ____
Behaviour: ____
Example: Sam grips the chair arm and goes quiet.

say.text: Hospital passports used in the UK ask for the same thing. They ask what the person looks like, sounds like and moves like when unwell or in pain.

show.text: What does pain look like for this person?

ask.q: Sam cannot say 'it hurts'. What helps staff most?
ask.right: A note on Sam's face, sounds and movements when Sam is in pain.
wrong: A note saying Sam is never in pain.
ask.why: Signs of pain are personal. A caregiver who has seen them can describe them.

say.text: Then add devices and what helps. List glasses, hearing aids, a speech device or a picture board. Say if the person needs extra time to answer.

show.text:
Devices: glasses, hearing aids, picture or letter board, speech device
Needs extra time to answer: yes / no
Best way to ask: short yes/no questions, one at a time

ask.q: What helps staff talk with a person who answers slowly?
ask.right: Give extra time and ask short yes/no questions, one at a time.
wrong: Talk only to the caregiver and ignore the person.
ask.why: Short yes/no questions are easier to answer. Staff should still speak to the person, not only to the caregiver.

say.text: Part two: allergies. List medicines, foods and anything else a doctor has named. Add what happens, if you know.

show.text:
Allergy: ____ What happens: ____
Allergy: ____ What happens: ____
If none are known, write: No known allergies

ask.q: Sam has no known allergies. What should the sheet say?
ask.why: A blank space looks like nobody checked. Writing 'no known allergies' shows you did.

say.text: Part three: medicines. Copy each one from its label. Add the dose, how often, what it is for, and how it is given.

show.text:
Name | strength | how much | when | what for | how given
Sample (invented): Medicine 1 | 10 mg | 1 tablet | morning | reason | by mouth

say.text: Include the over-the-counter ones, the vitamins and the supplements too. If you are unsure of a dose, ask the pharmacist to check the list.

show.text: Prescription AND over-the-counter AND vitamins

ask.q: Which belongs on the medicine list?
ask.right: Prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins and supplements, with dose and how often.
ask.why: Staff need the full picture, with doses, to avoid mix-ups.

say.text: A list only helps if it is current. The CDC's own list form says to update it any time you make a change.

ask.q: When should you update the medicine list?
ask.right: Any time a medicine or dose changes.
wrong: Once a year, on New Year's Day.
ask.why: An old list can mislead staff. The CDC says to update it whenever the medicines change.

say.text: That 40% is from one survey the CDC cited. It found that 40 percent could list all their prescription details if they were without their medicines in an evacuation.
Part four: conditions and doctors. Write the diagnoses in the words the doctors use. Add medical devices, the doctors' names and numbers, and the pharmacy.

show.text:
Conditions: ____
Medical devices (style, serial number): ____
Doctors and phone numbers: ____
Pharmacy: ____

ask.q: Why list the person's own doctors?
ask.right: So staff know who holds the person's medical history.
wrong: So staff do not need to treat the person.
So the doctors can skip the next visit.
It is only for tidy paperwork.
ask.why: The person's own doctors know the history. The sheet points staff to them. It does not replace them.

say.text: Part five: what is normal. Doctors call this baseline. It is the person's usual abilities, behaviour and signs.

show.text: Baseline = what is usual for this person

say.text: Why? A caregiver can say: this is how Sam usually is. Staff can then see what has changed.

show.text:
Usual for Sam: answers by blinking, sits up in a wheelchair, calm in the morning, likes the radio.
Not usual: unusually sleepy, quiet, restless or upset (example only).

ask.q: Why write down what is normal for the person?
ask.right: So staff can tell what has changed.
wrong: So staff can skip the exam.
So the person never needs an ER.
So the sheet replaces the doctor's notes.
ask.why: Staff meet the person once. You know the usual, so you can show the change.

say.text: Add what calms the person, what upsets them, and how they like to be addressed. A familiar voice or a favourite blanket can matter.

show.text:
What calms: ____
What upsets: ____
How to address me: ____
Who should stay with me: ____

say.text: Part six: contacts and who decides. List two people, in case the first does not answer. Say who decides if the person cannot, and where the paperwork is kept.

show.text:
Contact 1: ____ phone ____
Contact 2: ____ phone ____
Health care decision maker: ____
Paperwork kept at: ____

say.text: The decision maker is often called a health care agent or proxy. The rules differ by place. Ask the person's doctor, or check with your local resources.

show.text: Who decides? Rules vary by place.

ask.q: What goes on the sheet about the decision maker?
ask.right: Their name, their phone number, and where the paperwork is kept.
ask.why: Staff need a name and a number. They also need to know where to find the paperwork. Keep a copy where people can reach it.

say.text: Here is the whole page. The top half: name, communication, and allergies.

show.text:
NAME / likes to be called / date of birth / DATE UPDATED
HOW I COMMUNICATE: yes = ___ no = ___
PAIN OR DISTRESS LOOKS LIKE: ___
DEVICES AND WHAT HELPS: ___
ALLERGIES (and what happens): ___

say.text: The bottom half: medicines, conditions, what is normal, and contacts.

show.text:
MEDICINES: name | strength | how much | when | what for | how given
CONDITIONS and DEVICES: ___
DOCTORS and PHARMACY: ___
WHAT IS NORMAL: abilities, behaviour, usual signs, what calms
CONTACTS (two) and WHO DECIDES: ___ paperwork at ___

say.text: Where should copies live? In more than one place. Put one on the fridge, one in the go-bag, and a photo on your phone.

show.text:
Fridge or by the phone
Go-bag
Photo on your phone
With a trusted contact
Hand a copy to the crew or ER staff

say.text: A children's hospital advises keeping a copy with the emergency contact person too. Then someone else can find it.

show.text: More than one copy, in more than one place

ask.q: Where should copies of the sheet be kept?
ask.right: In more than one place, such as the fridge, the go-bag, your phone and with a trusted contact.
wrong: Only in a filing cabinet upstairs.
ask.why: Nobody knows where you will be in an emergency. Copies in several easy places are more likely to be found.

say.text: Update the page when anything changes: a medicine, a dose, a diagnosis, a doctor or a contact. Replace every copy, not just one. Also check it at medical visits.

show.text:
New or changed medicine
New condition or device
New doctor or contact
Check at each medical visit

ask.q: Sam's doctor changes a dose today. What do you do?
ask.right: Update the sheet and replace every copy.
wrong: Write the new dose on the fridge copy only.
ask.why: An out-of-date copy can mislead staff. Replace all of them.

say.text: A reminder. In an emergency, call 911 first. Grab the sheet only if it is quick. Never stop to fill it in or update it.

show.text: 911 first. The sheet second.

ask.q: Something frightening is happening. What comes first?
ask.right: Call 911, and grab the sheet only if it is quick.
wrong: Email the sheet to all the relatives.
ask.why: Getting help is the priority. The sheet can travel with the person afterwards.

say.text: To finish, ask the person's doctor or pharmacist to look over your sheet. Laws and services vary by place, so check with your local 911 center or fire department about what they offer.

show.text:
Ask the doctor or pharmacist to check it
Take a hands-on first-aid class (Red Cross, American Heart Association)
Check with your local 911 center or fire department

say.text: Your task: fill in just one part this week. Start with allergies, or with how the person says yes and no. Next class: the 911 card by the phone.

show.text:
This week: fill in one part
Next: Class 5, The 911 Card by the Phone and Telling Your Fire Department

notes.topic: How the person communicates (yes, no, pain)
Baseline: what is normal for this person

other_side.claim: The sheet should fit on one page.
other_side.other_view: The widely used AAP and ACEP Emergency Information Form is two pages, and families fill it in with the child's doctors. A one-page version is easier to read quickly. A longer form can hold more detail. Both approaches are used. Ask the person's own doctors which they prefer.

other_side.claim: A written list of medicines is enough to take to the ER.
other_side.other_view: One hospital guide says physicians prefer the actual medicine bottles. If you bring only a list, it must be up to date and include daily doses. So bring both if you can.

other_side.claim: Paper sheet versus a medical alert tag or bracelet.
other_side.other_view: FEMA suggests either medical alert tags or written descriptions of a disability and support needs. The emergency physicians' group also says children with special health needs should wear medical jewelry. The two work together. A tag is always on the person. A sheet holds far more detail.
